html:
Kabir was a weaver, poet and mystic of Varanasi in north India, one of the great voices of the bhakti movement. Tradition gives him the long span of 1398 to 1518; his real life probably fell within the 15th century.

He grew up in a family of Muslim weavers and may have learned from the Hindu teacher Ramananda. He belonged fully to neither faith. His short rhyming couplets, in plain Hindi, mock the priest and the mullah alike: the idols, the pilgrimages, the fasts, the call to prayer. God, for Kabir, has no form and lives inside each person.

His verses were passed on by singers before they were written down. They survive in three main collections:

  • The Bijak, kept by his followers in the Kabir Panth.
  • The Rajasthani Kabir Granthavali.
  • The Adi Granth of the Sikhs, which honours him beside Guru Nanak.

A well known legend says that at his death Hindus wanted to burn his body and Muslims to bury it, and when they lifted the shroud they found only flowers. He still speaks to people across both Hindu and Muslim India.
